Katalog Berita (Halaman 44/57)

#2752. Anthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spot

Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the tech industry is under mounting strain.

Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.

With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon, whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.

In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.

Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus. It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google, though delivery won't start until 2028.

"The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it."

Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.

By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.

The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.

"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."

Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.

"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.

Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.

It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.

Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds, which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.

Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress, who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.

The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.

Google will be paying particularly close attention.

The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf, which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said.

"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.

One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.

"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."

Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion.

That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.

"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."

#2751. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2750. Barlow ‘making progress,' Embiid out vs. Pacers, more on Sixers

Barlow 'making progress,' Embiid out vs. Pacers, more on Sixers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Dominick Barlow decided to finish his post-practice workout Saturday with a windmill dunk.

While Barlow remains out with a "lower back stress reaction" listing on the Sixers' injury report, it's one sign that he's trending up in his rehab process.

"He's making progress," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "He was a part of the practice today. It's kind of a game day type of practice … so it wasn't super intense, as you might expect. But he was out there doing some stuff. He's progressing. Just don't know when he'll be ready to go, but at least he's making some progress now."

Barlow was one of the Sixers' top role players last season, starting 59 games and contributing in a variety of areas. He averaged 7.7 points, 4.8 rebounds, 1.2 assists and 0.9 steals in 23.8 minutes per game.

"Size, athleticism, rebounding," Dean Wade said of the fifth-year forward. "He's another guy that can switch one through five."

Whenever the 6-foot-9 Barlow is available for his season debut, the Sixers will welcome him back as another option at center.

With Ariel Hukporti's preseason Achilles tendon tear and Adem Bona's cervical spine sprain, the team is light on healthy resources at the five. And Joel Embiid (right foot plantar fascia injury management) will sit Sunday afternoon vs. the Pacers on the first leg of a back-to-back. He'll presumably return to the lineup when the Sixers visit the Nets on Monday night.

"I think (Barlow) is probably going to have to play more five than we envisioned," Nurse said, "but Jabari (Walker) is doing that as well. If the situation calls for that, I imagine that's where he'll help the most."

With the Delaware Blue Coats hosting the Maine Red Claws on Friday and Saturday, the Sixers saw an opportunity for two players outside of the regular rotation to log minutes with their G League affiliate.

Rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. suited up Friday and third-year wing Justin Edwards played both games. Philon posted 20 points, nine rebounds and eight assists in a blowout loss. Edwards shot just 1 for 10 from the floor in the first game, but he scored 23 points on 9-for-17 shooting in Saturday's win.

Nurse has largely kept a tight rotation early in the season and the 10-3 Sixers haven't had many lopsided games with ample garbage time. As of Saturday night, the Sixers ranked 29th in the NBA in bench minutes per game.

"My first belief is it's hard to get better unless you're playing," Nurse said. "That kind of trumps everything, in my opinion. Just historically, we've had a number of guys that have gone down to those games, respected it … and it's really helped them in their careers. … It's been a minute for these guys — both of them — since they've had any real court time.

"So that fit into the schedule well. … I think it will also help them to just find some rhythm, find their legs a little bit. We're going to need everybody at some point, so keep 'em going."

VJ Edgecombe was among the crowd Friday night at Chase Fieldhouse.

"They're my brothers, man," he said. "Labaron, Justin, (Caleb Love), (Rayan Rupert). I just wanted to show love. … I didn't have (anything) to do yesterday. … We have that relationship off the court, too. I'm just being supportive and showing them that I care about them."

#2749. “Indescribably Worse”: NCAA Reporter Draws Attention to Geno Auriemma’s Behavior Before UConn’s Worst Loss in Nearly 2 Decades

Geno Auriemma has never been a quiet coach on the sideline. In 42 years at UConn, fans have gotten used to the raised voice, the hard stare, and the lecture, even when his team is winning big. But on Sunday night at Louisville, that version of Auriemma barely showed up. What showed up instead caught the attention of the reporters covering the game.

NCAA reporter Tyler DeLuca put it into words on X:

"We have seen a lot of Geno Auriemma loud scenes on the sidelines over the years. We aren't getting that tonight. It is the indescribably worse 'not mad just disappointed' energy that he is giving right now," DeLuca said.

He was watching No. 4 UConn suffer its worst loss in nearly two decades, a 69-51 defeat at No. 7 Louisville.

The game itself shows why a coach might go quiet. UConn never led, and the trouble started early. The Huskies scored only 16 points in the first half, their fewest in a half since the 2010 national title game against Stanford.

They made just 7-of-29 shots before the break, including 1-of-8 from three, and they gave the ball away 12 times. They went into the locker room trailing 30-16.

The second half brought no relief. Louisville led 55-29 early in the fourth quarter, and its biggest lead reached 26. UConn had only 29 points through three quarters, which AP called the worst in program history.

The Huskies shot a season-low 34% (21 of 61) for the game. They were outrebounded 51-30 and outscored 32-20 in the paint. They also committed 17 turnovers, which Louisville turned into 17 points.

Sarah Strong scored 19, and Ashlynn Shade and Jovana Popovic added 13 each, but she could not carry the team alone. UConn did hit half its shots (8 of 16) in the fourth quarter, though by then the game was long gone.

Geno Auriemma's silence showed up in the game too. He did not call a single timeout. He said the media timeouts were "very unproductive," so he felt, "why bother?" After the game, he described what it felt like to watch.

"As it was unfolding, you almost have a helpless feeling as you're watching it," Auriemma said.

It was a long night after the buzzer as well. He took the podium nearly 90 minutes after the game ended.

That is where DeLuca's comment starts to land, because Geno Auriemma has not always reacted this way. Less than two weeks earlier, in the season opener against Cornell, UConn was ahead by 35 points.

The game was long over, yet the cameras caught Auriemma telling his players that if they would not talk on defense, "you ain't playing Thursday night on the road." The Huskies won 100-35, and he was still demanding more.

Then came Michigan on Nov. 5. UConn lost 77-66, and Auriemma had plenty to say that night too. He called the performance "deeply disappointing" and said his team had lost its defensive integrity. In that loss, he could point to specific problems, and Strong's foul trouble gave the Huskies a clear reason for what went wrong. His frustration was loud, and it came with a list.

Sunday was different. There was no lecture, no list, and no timeouts. Geno Auriemma said the coaching staff was "stunned in the locker room" at what it saw. When he talked about the timeouts, he said you could tell in the players' faces that nothing he said was having any effect. That is the "not mad just disappointed" mood DeLuca described.

Louisville deserves credit for that, too. The Cardinals pushed the pace, controlled the glass and never let UConn settle in. It was UConn's first loss at Louisville since 2019 and its lowest-scoring game ever against the Cardinals.

UConn is now 3-2, which has happened only six times in Geno Auriemma's 42-year tenure.

He was already looking ahead after the game.

"You have to have a sense of urgency," he said, before adding, "We're a work in progress."

The schedule will not give the Huskies much room to breathe. They open Big East play against Seton Hall on Friday, and top-ranked South Carolina, No. 4 Duke, and No. 20 Maryland are all still on the way.

If the Cornell game showed Auriemma loud and demanding in a blowout win, Sunday showed the opposite. This time, the quiet may have said more than any lecture could.

#2748. China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin historic summit. What will be on the agenda?

China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders.

That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine.

While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025.

"For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors.

Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.

The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI.

The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda.

"He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call. The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.

Putin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.

Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.

China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election.

China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement.

"Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability."

A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship.

Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP.

U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

#2747. Tech world's calls for Jensen Huang to return to Nvidia are growing

An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia has drawn more than 160,000 signatures, as prominent tech executives, employees and shareholders rally behind the chipmaker's co-founder following his resignation last week.

The "Stand with Jensen" campaign has attracted support from Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, according to the petition's website, which notes that affiliations are self-reported and not verified.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993 and helped turn it into a dominant supplier of artificial intelligence chips, resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and board member last week following reports of extramarital affairs — including one involving a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor. The growing campaign to reinstate Huang adds a layer of complexity to the decision for Nvidia's board as it looks to put the controversy behind it, and coincides with reports that he is considering a comeback.

Any potential return, however, faces significant hurdles. Nvidia's board is continuing an independent investigation into the conduct that led to Huang's departure. What's more, U.S. lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged America's artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.

Musk was among the most prominent tech executives to publicly back Huang's reinstatement, saying on X that he would sign a petition calling for the former Nvidia chief's return.

"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X. He had previously also said it would be "an honor" to hire Huang.

The campaign has drawn support from people identifying themselves as current and former Nvidia employees, shareholders and business partners, according to the petition's website. It calls on Nvidia's board to ensure a fair investigation into Huang's conduct and provide greater transparency around the circumstances of his departure.

Some Nvidia employees have also publicly expressed support for Huang, with one engineer saying he had decided to leave the company following the CEO's departure.

Darrell Dai, who identified himself as a robotics engineer at Nvidia, said Huang's vision and the engineering culture he fostered were key reasons he had stayed at the company.

Another Nvidia employee, Vartika Singh, who said she had worked at the chipmaker for nearly eight years, praised Huang's leadership and personal support during a family medical crisis.

"I have never worked for anyone quite like Jensen Huang, and I doubt I ever will," Singh wrote on X, describing his commitment to employees, researchers and startups.

The push has also gained traction among major shareholders, with Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker urging Nvidia's board to consider all options, including Huang's potential return, in an open letter Friday.

The investors called for a measured approach to choosing Nvidia's next leader, arguing that Huang deserved a fair process before the board made any permanent decision.

Huang has discussed the possibility of returning as Nvidia's chief executive with close confidants, the Financial Times reported, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.

One of his allies told the FT that supporters were assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek backing from the White House.

The efforts had Huang's support, the person added, according to the report.

"We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the NVIDIA CEO role. We have not formally engaged any potential candidates," an Nvidia spokesperson said in response to CNBC's request for comment on the company's search.

The spokesperson added that any speculation about individual candidates, whether internal or external, was premature.

Anthony Scaramucci, founder of alternative investment firm SkyBridge and a former White House communications director, also dismissed the prospect of Huang returning as CEO, saying the investigations surrounding him presented obstacles that a public campaign could not overcome.

"The tech bros want Jensen back. Not happening," Scaramucci wrote on X, arguing that Nvidia's board could not reinstate a chief executive whose conduct remained under investigation.

In a separate post, Scaramucci rejected comparisons with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who returned to the company days after being ousted in 2023. "The FBI doesn't take petitions," he wrote, saying that Huang's situation was fundamentally different from Altman's. Altman's ouster stemmed from an internal governance dispute, while Huang's situation involves ongoing investigations into his conduct that make a swift board reversal far more difficult.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company linked to the controversy, said recent media reports contained assertions about its business and supply chain that were not supported by verifiable evidence.

The company said it had retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation and that Alice Huang, a woman reportedly romantically linked to Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and no longer holds any role there.

Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, CNBC reported earlier.

Meanwhile, Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Huang, the FT reported. Nvidia's board said at the time that it had not formally engaged any candidates.

Some analysts see a path for Huang to return despite the controversy surrounding his departure.

Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, said Huang could make a comeback if he overcomes his legal challenges, citing his influence in the AI industry and continued support from investors.

"If he can get through the legal trouble, I think we'll have a second act from him," Goldberg told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia."

But not everyone on Wall Street is convinced it can happen so soon.

"We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO," Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note.

Ives said the shareholder petition and public pressure could create further distractions for Nvidia, but would not change the central task facing interim CEO Kress: restoring stability and investor confidence.

Ives added that Nvidia's leadership in AI chips and its long-term demand outlook remained intact despite the management upheaval.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal third-quarter earnings Tuesday, putting Kress and the company's leadership team under the spotlight as investors look for reassurance about its future.

#2746. Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors

Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers will not need to wait long for an opportunity to move past their most lopsided loss of the season.

Less than 48 hours after Boston's 123-101 win exposed several of Philadelphia's early weaknesses, the Sixers will host the Toronto Raptors on Thursday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

The Raptors are coming off a difficult meeting with the Celtics, too. Toronto led Boston by 22 points Wednesday before being outscored 61-34 over the final 29:24 of a 98-93 loss.

Philadelphia enters at 9-3 following Tuesday's defeat. Toronto is 5-6 and will complete a back-to-back and its third game in four nights.

LeBron James has been ruled out because of low-back and sciatica management. Joel Embiid is questionable with right plantar fascia injury management. Toronto will be without Kawhi Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Nate Bittle.

Here are four areas to watch as the Sixers try to respond.

Few teams have forced opponents into mistakes as frequently as Toronto.

The Raptors have generated 18.9 turnovers per game, the highest mark in the NBA. They are also averaging 10.9 steals and nearly 15 offensive rebounds.

The Sixers have countered that type of pressure well. Their 13.0 turnovers per game are tied for one of the lowest marks in the league.

Toronto's length remains disruptive even without Leonard and Barnes. The Raptors regularly crowd ball handlers, reach into passing lanes and send multiple players toward the offensive glass. Jakob Poeltl supplies size inside while RJ Barrett, Ja'Kobe Walter and Collin Murray-Boyles can create problems away from the ball.

The Raptors' pressure can punish a careless pass twice. It takes away a Sixers possession and gives Toronto an opportunity to score before the defense gets organized.

Philadelphia has largely avoided those mistakes while adjusting to a new lineup and playing at a quicker pace. Maintaining that control without James, who has handled a significant share of the playmaking, will be one of Thursday's clearest challenges.

Toronto has not built its offense around half-court shooting.

The Raptors are averaging 49.6 paint points and 16.4 fast-break points. Even while shorthanded Wednesday, they scored 18 points in transition against Boston.

That presents a direct test for a Sixers defense allowing 16.5 fast-break points per game, the fourth-highest figure in the NBA. Philadelphia has also surrendered 49.5 paint points per contest.

The first concern will be slowing the ball.

Immanuel Quickley returned Wednesday after missing two games with right hamstring soreness. He gives Toronto another guard capable of attacking early in the shot clock, while Barrett has consistently looked to get downhill with Leonard and Barnes unavailable.

Poeltl can create scoring chances without having a play called for him. He runs the floor, screens for Toronto's guards, rolls toward the rim and cleans up misses.

The Sixers have been effective in transition themselves, averaging 17.1 fast-break points. Maxey and VJ Edgecombe can change ends quickly after a stop, but Philadelphia must secure the ball first.

Thursday's game could swing on which team gets to run and which one is forced to create against a set defense.

Toronto provided an extreme example Wednesday of how quickly the three-point line can alter a game.

The Raptors entered their matchup against Boston shooting 31.8 percent from beyond the arc. They proceeded to hit 10 of their 18 attempts in the first quarter, tying a franchise record for threes in a period.

They went 6 for 25 over the final three quarters.

After Wednesday, Toronto is shooting 32.4 percent from three this season. The Sixers should not treat the Raptors like an elite perimeter team. They also cannot allow them to find early confidence through uncovered catch-and-shoot attempts.

Walter made five threes Wednesday and scored a team-high 17 points. Rookie Allen Graves added 13 points, while Quickley, Barrett and Jamison Battle are all willing shooters when the ball reaches them in rhythm.

Philadelphia's problems against Boston extended beyond the Celtics making difficult shots. The Sixers were late on several closeouts and occasionally allowed too much separation while navigating screens.

Toronto does not rely on the three as heavily as Boston. Wednesday showed it can still build a lead quickly when those shots start falling.

The Raptors expended significant energy Wednesday before traveling to Philadelphia.

They scored 38 first-quarter points, built a 22-point lead and then watched Boston erase the entire margin before the end of the third quarter. Quickley and Barrett each played more than 31 minutes. Poeltl and Walter both played at least 29.

The Sixers should have the fresher legs. Whether they take advantage could become apparent early.

Philadelphia has averaged 26.3 first-quarter points with a minus-2.2 scoring margin in opening periods. Slow starts have forced the Sixers to play from behind several times, including in their 29-point comeback against Cleveland.

An aggressive start would make Toronto respond quickly after a draining loss. Maxey and Edgecombe can apply pressure by pushing the ball after defensive rebounds instead of allowing the Raptors to set their pressure defense.

James' absence will require an adjustment. Maxey, Brown and Anfernee Simons should handle more of the ball and more of the decisions that come with initiating the offense.

If Embiid plays, the Sixers can make Toronto work through Poeltl by establishing him inside. If Embiid sits, Philadelphia's size concerns will become more pronounced with Adem Bona, Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti also unavailable.

The Sixers have a rest advantage against a depleted opponent coming off an emotional loss. Their response should begin well before the fourth quarter.

#2745. Browns’ cardiac act sets them apart from any other team in NFL history

Browns' cardiac act sets them apart from any other team in NFL history appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Cleveland Browns continue to find ways to win close games, taking down the Houston Texans 27-24 in another closely contested affair on Sunday in Week 10. Despite falling behind 17-0, Todd Monken's team rallied for its sixth victory of the season, becoming the first team in NFL history to have each of its first six wins decided by four points or fewer, according to ESPN Research.

Houston scored touchdowns on its first three possessions before the Browns responded with 20 unanswered points to take a 20-17 advantage late in the third quarter. However, after kicker Andre Szmyt missed a long field goal, the Texans capitalized on a defensive pass interference penalty against cornerback Myles Harden and regained the lead with an 11-yard touchdown pass.

Cleveland, led by quarterback Deshaun Watson, eventually came up with the defining counterpunch. Watson connected with tight end Harold Fannin Jr. for a 30-yard completion that moved the Browns to Houston's five-yard line, allowing running back Quinshon Judkins to score the go-ahead touchdown on the following play. The Texans had one final opportunity with 47 seconds remaining, but quarterback CJ Stroud's fourth-down attempt fell incomplete.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Watson completed 25 of 40 passes for 312 yards and a touchdown while adding 49 rushing yards and another score on eight carries. Fannin finished with seven receptions for 91 yards.

Watson also recorded his third consecutive 300-yard passing performance and surpassed 20,000 career passing yards. The victory also marked his sixth game-winning drive this season, tying Watson with Bo Nix for the NFL lead. It also tied him with Bernie Kosar for the second-most game-winning drives by a Browns quarterback in a single season, behind Brian Sipe's seven.

The Browns have secured four double-digit comeback wind, tying the league record for the most through a team's first 10 games in a season. Additionally, their 6-4 record has surpassed the preseason projected win total of 5.5, while their 4-0 home start is their first such run since 1963.

Cleveland now enters its Week 11 bye before returning on November 29 to host the Las Vegas Raiders, carrying considerable momentum into the final seven games.

#2743. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2741. Always one of a kind, Oubre reflects on Sixers stint, why he chose Pacers

Always one of a kind, Oubre reflects on Sixers stint, why he chose Pacers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Kelly Oubre Jr. experience switched sides Sunday afternoon at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

Back in Philadelphia with the visiting Pacers, Oubre was his usual self. There's never any risk of mistaking Oubre for somebody else.

"Love him," Pacers head coach Rick Carlisle said pregame. "Such an upbeat guy. He's such a unique person. Love the wardrobe, all the different stuff. He's a very authentically one-of-a-kind type guy."

Carlise then detailed Oubre's various basketball qualities, some of which he showed in Indiana's 131-124 loss. The 30-year-old lefty wing scored 16 points and grabbed four rebounds. His day also included a theatrical imitation of Jaylen Brown's off-arm push after the Sixers' star was whistled for an offensive foul.

Sixers fans grew familiiar with Oubre's strengths, weaknesses and eccentricities during his three seasons as a Sixer. He wound up becoming the team's third-longest tenured player behind only Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey. Oubre played 178 regular-season games and averaged 14.9 points, 5.4 rebounds, 1.6 assists and 1.3 steals.

After the Sixers replaced president of basketball operations Daryl Morey with Mike Gansey, Oubre signed a two-year contract with the Pacers in free agency.

"Mike came over from Cleveland and I heard whispers that he wanted some of his Cleveland guys," Oubre said before the game in in the visitors' locker room. "And I was like, 'OK, cool. I'm a Philly guy. So I guess when he comes over, I will no longer be a Philly guy.' That was kind of the situation at hand.

"No bad blood because business is business at the end of the day. They have a great team over there, and they put together a team that they think is the best for them. I'll be all right elsewhere. I figured it out."

Oubre thought Indiana made sense as his next stop.

"It was the pace, the culture, the attitude that this team has," he said. "It's a fast-paced style of basketball. It's a bunch of guys who work collectively as a unit and kind of figure it out from there.

"I thought that would be a great opportunity for me to come and and kind of free-flow play, not have to think. I was wrong. Been thinking a lot, but I'm starting to figure it out and starting to get my rhythm here. … It's a great culture. Coach Rick Carlisle is a legend, Hall of Fame coach. And they wanted me. I love people who want me."

As Oubre settled into a new city, the Sixers had a stunning, transformational summer.

Gansey traded for Jaylen Brown, signed LeBron James, and added veteran role players like (former Cavalier) Dean Wade, Anfernee Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope. Oubre followed along.

"It was must-see TV, like (for) everybody else," he said. "As a basketball fan, it was pretty cool to see where I was kind of reinvent and get new life and new energy. So I was happy with that. Would I have loved to be a part of it? Of course.

"But at the end of the day, I'm a grown man and I've got to keep it moving and figure it out for myself. It was entertaining. … I'm kind of happy for all the people that have sacrificed over these years. … I'm trying to put a road block in that road for y'all."

Oubre joined the Sixers on a minimum-salary deal in September of 2023 after averaging 20.3 points the past season with the Hornets. Head coach Nick Nurse pitched Oubre on his potential to be a valuable, multi-dimensional player for good teams.

"I was literally about to be done with basketball," he said. "Coach Nurse called me multiple times and said, 'I want you to play for me.' And I was like, 'You know what? This guy really seems to care. He really wants me.' So thank you for just pulling me out of that pit and that hole that I was in four years ago. I got some new life in my basketball career.

"I'm always thankful for that and I love Nurse for that. Just appreciative for my time here. The battle wounds and scars that I've been able to build up, it made me a better man."

Throughout his Sixers stint, Oubre often spoke of growth, evolution, adaptation and self-discovery.

He talked again Sunday about his desire to "Be water" and how life as a Sixer changed him.

"I grew a lot, man," Oubre said. "Just the mental fortitude of being able to withstand adversity. Being able to wake up and not necessarily know which soliders are going to battle, just having to put on different hats on any given night. At first it was challenging, because I'm thinking about all the logistics and things and like, 'This is not what they asked me to do.' But at the end of the day, I just bought into being somebody that can be like water and grow with the team.

"It's been a blessing to be able to play with (VJ Edgecombe), be able to watch Tyrese (Maxey) ascend. Those are the guys where we were front line a lot. Just going through war with those guys was amazing. It just taught me mental fortitude. If I can make it through this, I can make it through anything."

Oubre felt he developed a meaningful connection with the Philadelphia fan base over his three years.

"When they talk about the City of Brotherly Love, I think they're talking about your soul, not necessarily about what you can offer them and what you do," he said. "Everybody in this city works hard. They wake up, go to work, keep the city going. And us as the prima donna basketball players, the least we can do is go hard and sacrifice for them so that they have something to cheer about when they come home from work.

"I think that was the relationship that we had. I'm forever indebted and forever grateful to the people in the city of Philadelphia."

#2740. UFC 334 Main Card Recap: Ciryl Gane Outlasts Josh Hokit In Record-Breaking Heavyweight War

UFC 334 marked the promotion's 10th event at Madison Square Garden, and it certainly delivered a memorable night of action. The UFC first visited the world's most famous arena in 2016 for UFC 205, an historic event headlined by Conor McGregor, who made history by becoming the promotion's first simultaneous two-division champion. Since then, the company has returned to the iconic New York venue with a major November event every year, with just one exception.

This year was no different, as the promotion put together two blockbuster title fights to headline its latest visit to Madison Square Garden. Ciryl Gane put his heavyweight championship on the line against Josh Hokit, while Kayla Harrison defended her women's bantamweight title against former two-division champion Amanda Nunes.

The five-fight main card featured five compelling stories, each with its own talking points. Let's break them down one by one.

The 25-year-old Bilal Hasan entered with an undefeated 10-0 record and a huge hype behind him. Some betting odds placed him as a -1100 to -1200 favorite.

Luis Gurule entered the fight with relatively little attention. But that lack of attention might have helped him to keep his composure, because he put on a really good, and strategic performance.

The 32-year-old flyweight endured Hasan's dynamic striking in the beginning and later even got a nasty cut. However, he used his wrestling to control the hot prospect and edge out a split decision victory.

Uros Medic and Kevin Holland were set to throw down and they did to a certain extent but fate had some other plans for them. Holland started with his slick striking mixed with offensive grappling in the first round. He continued his approach in the second, but had to take a long break due to getting hit on the groin repeatedly. Referee took a point from Medic for the unintentional but repetitive low blows.

The consensus scoring was going Holland's way as they entered the third round. Serbian might've won the final round with his aggression but still it was also close. However, the judges saw a different story. One judge scored the fight 29-27 for Medic, while the other two had it 29-29, leading to a majority draw.

There was some confusion in the post fight but the final verdict remains the same. make it better

This middleweight fight looked like a grappler vs striker affair on paper, and it went precisely like that.

Yousri Belgaroui had some moments to showcase his kickboxing prowess but other than that, Caio Borralho led most of the fight with his clinch and ground control. The Brazilian took a unanimous decision (30-27 across the cards) victory over the Dutchman and kept his place in the top 10 of the middleweight rankings.

Many billed the clash between Kayla Harrison and Amanda Nunes as the greatest women's MMA fight of all time, given the remarkable accomplishments both women have achieved in combat sports.

Nunes was returning to the Octagon after a three-year retirement, while Harrison was making her comeback following surgery for a serious neck injury.

The fight lived up to the hype for as long as it lasted, with both women having their moments. Nunes made a strong start, showcasing her trademark power and elite distance management. However, as the fight progressed, 'The Lioness' increasingly engaged Harrison in grappling exchanges rather than relying on her striking from range. That decision cost her valuable control time.

It appeared Nunes was determined to prove she could outgrapple a two-time Olympic judo gold medalist, but the strategy ultimately backfired. In the fourth round, Harrison capitalised on an opening, took Nunes' back, and locked in a rear-naked choke to secure the submission victory.

Harrison retained her UFC women's bantamweight crown and also earned the bragging rights to call herself one of the greatest.

Madison Square Garden got exactly what it came for as Ciryl Gane and Josh Hokit delivered a relentless, record-breaking heavyweight showdown.

Hokit lived up to his promise of constant forward pressure across all five rounds, but Gane's superior technique and precision allowed him to outpoint the aggressive challenger and retain his title.

The heavyweight title fight began with Hokit shooting for an early takedown. From there, 'The Incredible Hok' relentlessly pushed the pace, turning the opening three rounds into an all-out dogfight. He constantly marched forward, mixing his boxing with wrestling to keep Gane under pressure.

However, the champion showcased his improved takedown defense and remained composed throughout the exchanges, landing the cleaner and more powerful strikes to counter Hokit's aggression.

The opening three rounds were closely contested and could have gone either way, depending on whether one valued Gane's precise, high-volume striking or Hokit's relentless punching combinations and grappling control. However, the momentum shifted in the championship rounds as Hokit visibly began to slow down, while Gane stuck to his game plan and continued landing the more significant strikes.

After a phenomenal five-round heavyweight battle, the judges awarded Gane a unanimous decision victory (48-47), allowing the champion to successfully defend his undisputed title for the first time.

The fight set a new record for the most significant strikes landed in a UFC heavyweight bout, with Gane and Hokit combining for an astonishing 383 significant strikes. Gane also etched his name in the record books, surpassing Daniel Cormier's previous benchmark of 237 significant strikes landed in a single UFC heavyweight bout.

#2738. Purdy, McCaffrey lead 49ers offense in win vs Cowboys: winners, losers

The San Francisco 49ers offense was just about unstoppable against the Dallas Cowboys in their Week 10 matchup.

The Niners put up 584 yards against the Cowboys on the way to a 46-40 win on Nov. 15 at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas.

San Francisco quarterback Brock Purdy had another MVP-like performance, throwing for a career-high 389 yards, completing 22-of-28 passes for three touchdowns. But he wasn't the only one to notch a career-high. Niners running back Christian McCaffrey had his best day as a receiver catching four passes for a 161 yards (career-high) and two touchdowns. Deebo Samuel Sr. had 109 total yards and two touchdowns on the day.

The Cowboys defense pulled a no-show, but their offense wasn't too shabby. Dallas gained 439 total yards on offense as quarterback Dak Prescott tossed five touchdowns on 30-for-51 passes for 343 yards. Most of their damage was caused by George Pickens, who went off for 11 catches, 145 yards and three touchdowns.

The 49ers defense fended off the Cowboys when it mattered to advance to 8-1 on the season. Their Week 11 matchup is against the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City on Nov. 22, while the Cowboys face the the Tennessee Titans ahead of their annual Thanksgiving Day game.

49ers quarterback continues to have a scorching-hot 2026 season, leading San Francisco to the best record in the NFC. Against the Cowboys, in his first appearance at AT&T Stadium, Purdy didn't disappoint. Matter of fact, he went out for a career-high in passing yards with 389 in the win. He remains undefeated against the Cowboys, now 4-0, including the postseason.

Purdy put some good clips on the tape against the Cowboys. One play he danced in the pocket before escaping, extending the play, to find Christian McCaffrey across the middle who took it 74 yards for a score in the second quarter.

In the third quarter, the Niners drew up an end around play that saw Deebo Samuel Sr. out in the open field with Purdy as a lead blocker. He did just enough for Samuel to flip into a 70-yard touchdown.

Christian McCaffrey is one of the best dual threat running backs of all-time. He showed why he's a cheat code against the Cowboys. He had three total touchdowns. On the ground, he went for 13 carries, 62 yards and a touchdown. McCaffrey had a career-high 161 receiving yards, including a 74-yard score which was the longest catch-and-run in his career.

He also scored his eighth consecutive rushing touchdown, passing Joe Dorsey's record that spanned across the 1953-54 seasons. He's been a valuable asset to the Niners offense providing them with a dependable touchdown machine out the backfield.

Niners rookie Kaelon Black is making the most of his touches out the backfield sharing carries with McCaffrey. Black had a solid outing against the Cowboys going 11 carries, 53 yards and a touchdown.

His 25-yard rushing touchdown was arguably the run of the game, maybe the week. Black found the endzone but not before running through a couple of Cowboys defenders along the way. It was the type of smash mouth football that you love to see from your second-string back, let alone a rookie.

He has 79 carries for 356 yards and two touchdowns in his first season. He averages 4.5 yards per carry.

When it comes to some of the best fans, and well-traveled many think of the Raiders, Cowboys, Steelers and Packers. However, you have to mention the 49ers' fanbase, at least you do after how they showed up in Arlington, Texas. Members of the FOX broadcast mentioned how loud, and present, the 49ers fans were at AT&T Stadium. It sounded like they were playing at Levi's Stadium.

If there's any place of concern after the Niners' win against the Cowboys, it's in their secondary. The caveat is that their starting cornerbacks were questionable to play going into the game. However, both stuck it out. Renardo Green finished with seven total tackles while Deommodore Lenoir had five tackles and four pass deflections.

Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott threw for 343 yards, but wide receiver George Pickens went off for 11 catches, 145 yards and three touchdowns. CeeDee Lamb had a rather quiet game, but still effective with seven catches, 72 yards and a touchdown.

Lenoir took responsibility after the game saying, "I got to play better. They paid me to make plays."

The Cowboys defense took the biggest "L" of the day. They were historically bad, allowing the 49ers to go for 584 total yards. It was the most yards allowed at AT&T Stadium. The 49ers scored three touchdowns of at least 60 yards from scrimmage, which tied for the most by a team in a game over the last 50 years, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.

#2737. Carson Beck on his first start: It was cool, but losing is awful

Carson Beck started his first NFL game Sunday. It didn’t go as he had hoped, but the lights weren’t too bright for the Cardinals’ rookie quarterback.

“The ebbs and flows of football, I’ve been through it,” Beck said, via Darren Urban of the team website. “Not at this level. But it’s still the same game that we play. I’ve been through the good, the bad, the ugly, the uglier.

“How are you able to respond when things go bad? Obviously, we didn’t respond well today, and that starts with me. . . . But having the opportunity to play, that’s what allows us to stay focused. To be out there is fun. Football is fun.”

Beck went 11-of-18 for 108 yards and two interceptions in the 34-6 loss to the Rams. The Cardinals had only 123 yards and six first downs.

Coach Mike LaFleur said Beck did everything they asked him to do but conceded it was “a rough day” for the offense.

“It was cool,” Beck said. “Losing is awful. Don’t get it twisted. Losing is the worst thing ever. I hate losing. I haven’t done a lot of it. But it’s not about me. It’s about the team, and what we can do to fix the things to win games like this.

“But it was awesome. Going out on the first drive, looking across the field at guys like Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett. I just smiled for a second and was like, ‘This is sick.’ This is the thing you dream of when you start playing football at 6, 7 years old.”

#2736. Warriors Eyeing 2 Replacements For Kristaps Porzingis; Potential Trade Offers To Land The Targets

Coming off their most recent 123-85 loss to the San Antonio Spurs, the Golden State Warriors will have a lot of questions that need to be addressed. While these will primarily revolve around how they will manage in Stephen Curry's absence, doubts about their big man rotation will continue to plague the team.

With Kristaps Porzingis stepping away from basketball, the Golden State Warriors face a significant shortfall in their center rotation. Although players such as Charles Bassey, Al Horford, and Draymond Green have served as backup options, the Warriors clearly need an upgrade.

For the most part, it is a well-established fact that Golden State has been looking to offload Porzingis in a trade. As the Dubs continue their search for a replacement, ClutchPoints' Brett Siegel recently revealed two players who are supposedly on Golden State's radar. He shared:

"The two names that we're paying attention to for the Warriors, that we have been paying attention to for months in terms of frontcourt talent, [are] Wendell Carter Jr., like we mentioned last week, for the Orlando Magic, a possible guy that they could look to salary dump to free up some cap space on their end."

"And then also Naz Reid with the Charlotte Hornets. He was traded from the Minnesota Timberwolves to the Charlotte Hornets this past offseason. He's had a ton of suitors between the Warriors, the Portland Trail Blazers, and a few other teams mixed in there."

Both Naz Reid and Wendell Carter Jr. are players that have been generating more interest in the trade market. While Reid has certainly attracted more attention from suitors, especially in light of recent reports, there is reason to believe that both he and Carter could be viable targets for Golden State.

But how exactly would the Warriors acquire them?

Golden State Warriors Receive: Wendell Carter Jr.

Orlando Magic Receive: Kristaps Porzingis, 2031 second-round pick

Wendell Carter Jr. positions himself as a serviceable big man. Although undersized compared to Porzingis, the 6'10" big man possesses remarkable strength and the necessary tools to be a reliable interior presence on both ends of the floor.

This season, the 27-year-old is averaging 13.5 points, 9.3 rebounds, 1.0 steals, and 0.8 blocks per game while shooting 60.4% from the field and 40.0% from three-point range. With offensive versatility and defensive flexibility, at a price tag of $18.1 million, Carter is a steal. Hence, to acquire him, the Warriors would have to get creative.

For starters, the Dubs would have to capitalize on the Orlando Magic's current cap situation. With a total payroll of $219.1 million, the Magic are just $2.5 million below the first apron. While this is decent enough for now, when the time comes to retain some players next summer, the Magic will not view this situation favorably.

To improve their flexibility, the Warriors could present the idea of acquiring Kristaps Porzingis as a functional trade exception. By withholding his $20 million contract this year, and with only $3 million guaranteed next year, the Magic would be shedding a considerable amount of salary. This would allow them to make the necessary moves to retain players like Anthony Black.

For obvious reasons, Orlando may be hesitant to make this deal. However, by floating a second-round pick, or even a first-round pick based on how desperate they are, the Warriors may be able to tempt Orlando into accepting the offer.

Charlotte Hornets Receive: Kristaps Porzingis, Gui Santos, 2031 second-round pick

From a fit perspective, both Naz Reid and Wendell Carter Jr. have the potential to be key players in the Warriors' rotation. However, when gauging Reid's overall offensive upside, one could argue that he could be more impactful.

Since joining the Charlotte Hornets, the 27-year-old has had the freedom to showcase another layer of his game. With averages of 17.3 points (career-high), 8.5 rebounds, 2.2 assists, and 0.8 steals per game, Reid has not only demonstrated his ability to score but also his capacity to create chances for himself. This makes him a valuable asset.

At $23.2 million, acquiring Reid would require the Warriors to part with more than just Porzingis, primarily to avoid taking on more salary and crossing the second apron. Hence, packaging Porzingis with Gui Santos' $4.6 million contract and a second-round pick may be the only way to execute this deal for the Dubs.

For Charlotte, this trade has no significant consequences. Given their trade exceptions, any incoming contracts would have a negligible effect on their overall cap space. In addition to this, their rebuilding outlook allows them to prioritize draft picks, future cap flexibility, and young assets, all of which can be gained in this scenario.

Theoretically, a trade of this nature has some merit. Given what Naz Reid brings to the table, the Warriors could stand to benefit from his positional versatility. Conversely, however, given how similar Reid is to Yaxel Lendeborg, the Dubs may see parting with a developing asset like Santos for another player of the same template as counterintuitive.

While the interest in Naz Reid is noteworthy, the Warriors may need to gauge what their priorities are. However, despite Reid's upside, there may be more merit for Golden State to pursue a player like Wendell Carter Jr. to solidify their interior.

#2735. Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win

Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers brushed off their blowout loss to the Celtics and got back in the win column Thursday night.

They overcame a first-quarter deficit as high as 17 points and earned a 123-112 home win over the Raptors. The Sixers moved to 10-3 and Toronto fell to 5-7.

Tyrese Maxey had 27 points and eight assists. Joel Embiid added 20 points.

Jaylen Brown tallied 18 points and six rebounds. VJ Edgecombe posted 15 points, eight rebounds and a season-high eight assists. Anfernee Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range.

RJ Barrett recorded 31 points and 14 rebounds. Immanuel Quickley had 26 points and six assists.

The Sixers were without LeBron James (low back/sciatica management), Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear).

The team told reporters Thursday morning that Bona will be re-evaluated in approximately one week and that Barlow participated in shootaround. The 23-year-old forward also went through a pregame workout on the Xfinity Mobile Arena floor. There's no formal timetable for his return.

Toronto's sidelined players included Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes.

The Sixers will face the Pacers on Sunday afternoon in Philadelphia. Here are observations on their victory over the Raptors:

Dean Wade began the game in James' normal spot. The Sixers started slowly, missing their first foul field goals and opening 1 for 8 from three-point range.

He stayed down after setting a ball screen and having an apparent knee-to-knee collision with Ja'Kobe Walter. The Sixers called timeout with 8:30 left in the first quarter and Embiid grabbed at his right knee. He eventually rose with assistance from teammates and Sixers head athletic trainer Kevin Johnson, then limped back to the locker room. Jabari Walker entered.

At the 5:26 mark of the first quarter, Embiid checked back in to cheers from the home fans.

"I knew that he didn't twist it or anything," Maxey said. "I knew it was a knee-to-knee, so I wasn't too worried. He kept saying, 'I just got kneed.' That still hurts, though."

Embiid ended up logging 28 minutes, though he certainly wanted to play more.

"He was very, very motivated to play," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "It was hard to get him out for his scheduled rests tonight, which is a good problem sometimes."

While Embiid's return was a major positive development, the Sixers fell further behind. The Raptors' lead swelled to 32-16 with a Jamison Battle three-pointer and Nurse burned a timeout.

Simons sunk a buzzer-beating three to conclude the first quarter, cutting the Sixers' deficit to nine points.

"Those are big momentum plays that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment," Nurse said.

The Sixers kept rolling against a shorthanded Toronto team playing on the second night of a back-to-back. Simons nailed a triple to kick off the scoring in the second quarter. Brown buried a mid-range jumper and Edgecombe jammed in a crowd-pleasing dunk to give the Sixers a 35-34 edge.

Brown and Edgecombe shined in the second quarter both as individuals and as a duo. The Sixers need Edgecombe to attack a bit more offensively when he shares the floor with Brown and bench players. It doesn't hurt for the second-year guard to have that clarity about his role in those units.

"He's one of our better playmakers," Maxey said of Edgecombe. "He's really good at getting downhill and creating for himself and others."

The Sixers' only three bench rotation players were Walker, Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope (11 points, five assists). In addition to Walker, Wade got center minutes behind Embiid.

Embiid picked up his third foul with 2:23 left in the second quarter and had to take a seat. The teams were tied at 60 apiece through two periods.

The game remained even for much of the third, but Maxey fueled an 11-0 Sixers run late in the quarter.

His speed and the Sixers' collective focus on pushing the pace whenever possible allowed the team to get regular points before Toronto could set its defense. Maxey zoomed in for a layup, then tossed the ball ahead to Brown for an easy bucket. Brown assisted a Simons three. Walker converted a fast-break lay-in and canned a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter. All of a sudden, the Sixers held a 101-87 lead.

Brown, Edgecombe and the bench gave the Sixers more good minutes early in the fourth quarter. They sealed the deal without any late drama. And the fans chanting for a Tacko Fall appearance got their wish with a final-minute entrance by the 7-foot-6 center.

#2734. Joe Burrow matches Peyton Manning's record for consecutive games with at least four TDs

Joe Burrow has accomplished something that had not been done for over 20 years.

With his 4-yard touchdown to Chase Brown in the third quarter, Burrow became the first since Peyton Manning in 2004 to have at least four total touchdowns in five consecutive games, which is the longest streak in NFL history.

That score gave the Bengals a commanding 31-3 lead with 4:12 left in the third period.

Burrow has been excellent all season, but that's particularly been the case on Sunday night. So far, he's completed 32-of-41 passes for 359 yards with four TDs.

The one difference between Manning's streak and Burrow's is that Manning did it with all passing touchdowns. Between Weeks 8 and 12 in 2004, Manning threw for five, four, five, four, and six TDs with the Colts.

Manning would win his second MVP award for his 2004 season.

Burrow has thrown for four, four, five, three, and now four in his last six games. He's also had a rushing touchdown in each of the last two weeks before Sunday's matchup against Pittsburgh.

#2721. ‘Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles

'Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker shared the floor for 128 games in Portland. The Trail Blazers won 43 of them.

They sat beside one another in the Sixers' interview room Thursday night after a victory and discussed what the other 85 taught them.

"Whether you've got a big role or a small role, it's hard to win in the NBA," Simons said. "We've seen it firsthand."

Their roles were considerably different then.

Simons was an established starter entrusted with creating and scoring. Walker, a 2022 second-round pick, was trying to establish himself in a rotation. During their three overlapping seasons, Portland went 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46. The Blazers missed the playoffs each year.

Both are now reserves on a Sixers team constructed to contend. In nine games they've both appeared in this season, Philadelphia is 7-2.

They provided 26 points, 11 rebounds and six three-pointers in the Sixers' 123-112 win over the Raptors at Xfinity Mobile Arena. Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range. Walker recorded nine points and eight rebounds, including four on the offensive glass.

The Sixers outscored Toronto by 24 points during Simons' 23 minutes. Neither former Blazer committed a turnover.

Their production helped Philadelphia overcome a 17-point first-quarter deficit and improve to 10-3 without LeBron James.

"You learn once you come off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there," Simons said. "Obviously, we started off kind of slow. You just want to go in, bring some energy, get some stops, get out and run. I think everybody who got off the bench brought energy."

Simons supplied an immediate lift with a deep three-pointer at the first-quarter buzzer. His shot ended an 8-0 Sixers run and trimmed Toronto's lead to nine.

He remained involved during an 11-0 burst late in the third quarter, knocking down a three and setting up Walker for a basket. Walker then made a three early in the fourth before Simons scored on the Sixers' next possession.

When Toronto pulled within six with less than five minutes remaining, Simons answered with his fifth three-pointer.

Making those shots is the most obvious way Simons can help a roster already featuring James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown. He said the Sixers have not made him feel as though every opportunity must go in.

"They encourage us to keep shooting the ball," Simons said. "Knowing that a team has that much confidence in us to keep shooting makes the game that much easier. Whether you miss or make, as long as we get the right shots in the right moments, I think everybody can live with the misses and makes."

Simons spent seven seasons in Portland before playing last year with Boston and Chicago. His move to Philadelphia reunited him with Walker and Rayan Rupert, another former Blazer who joined the Sixers on a two-way contract during the offseason.

Knowing familiar faces awaited him helped Simons enter another new locker room.

"It made the transition seamless," he said. "Just being able to have some comfortability with guys that I played with for multiple years. It's been fun, kind of feeling like a little bit of old times. Me, Bari and Rups have been through a lot."

Walker's path to Philadelphia began a year earlier and required an additional step.

After playing 188 games over three seasons with Portland, Walker signed a two-way contract with the Sixers in July 2025. He earned a standard contract in February and has since pushed his way into the backup-center conversation despite standing 6-foot-7.

Walker believes some of the work he did on losing teams was easily missed.

"When I first got to the league, I was part of a rebuilding process," he said. "I just felt like some of the little things I did didn't always get noticed when you're losing. I told myself, if I ever got to be part of a winning organization, then I'd go out and expand my abilities."

Rebounding has made Walker difficult for Nick Nurse to overlook.

Walker credited his timing and strong hands to lessons passed down by his father, former NBA center Samaki Walker. Those instincts have become especially useful while the Sixers piece together their frontcourt behind Embiid.

"Rebounding is a skill I kind of honed in on," Walker said. "My dad was a good rebounder. He was known for his rebounding and his timing. I think it's just a gift that he transferred to me."

Walker has made it clear that he expected to earn a role this season.

"I don't know if I was delusional, but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part," he said. "I read something where they said it's a surprise, but if you were around me this summer, it wouldn't be a surprise. This is expected, and I just want to continue to get better."

The freedom Simons once had in Portland is no longer necessary. Walker does not need a high volume of touches, either. Both understand that playing beside the Sixers' stars requires shooting when open, moving the ball and handling the less glamorous work.

"You've got to find ways to impact the game multiple ways, even if you're not scoring," Simons said. "Whether it's cutting, making the right read and pass to Joel, being the right swing pass to VJ, boxing out on defense or just being in the right position."

Their opportunities will fluctuate. Simons may take nine shots one night and only a few the next. Walker's minutes will depend on matchups and the health of Philadelphia's frontcourt.

Winning has changed what they are being asked to do. Their three years together in Portland taught them why the adjustment is worthwhile.

"You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning," Simons said. "That's something you can't take for granted."
